Sums of Two Squares

Number TheoryCoordinatesUnit Distance Problem
Game: Pick a number and see every way to write it as one square plus another, as dots on a circle.
How to play: Slide the number, or press the button to jump to the next number with more ways than any before.

Look for the math

A dot of the whole-number grid at (a, b) is on the circle of radius √n exactly when a² + b² = n. Counting these dots is counting the ways to write n as a sum of two squares.

Jacobi's count

Count signs and order, so that 25 = 5² + 0² gives 4 dots and 25 = 4² + 3² gives 8: that is 12 in all. In general the number of dots is 4 (d₁ − d₃), where d₁ and d₃ count the divisors of n that leave remainder 1 and 3 when divided by 4. The test compares this with a direct count for every n up to 1200.

Primes decide it

Factor n. If some prime that leaves remainder 3 mod 4 appears an odd number of times, there are no dots at all (3, 6, 7, 11 …). Otherwise the count is 4 times the product of (e + 1) over the primes p ≡ 1 mod 4, where e is the power of p. So 25 = 5² gives 4 · 3 = 12, and 65 = 5 · 13 gives 4 · 2 · 2 = 16. The records come from stacking small primes that are 1 mod 4: 5, 65, 325, 1105 …

From dots to unit distances

Shrink the grid by 1/√n. Every grid point then has a unit-distance neighbour for each dot on the circle, so r₂(n) of them. On a k × k piece of this grid with n picked well, the number of unit pairs is about the number of points times r₂(n), and since r₂ can be made larger than any power of log, Erdős got n1 + C / log log n unit distances for n points. The next pages put this into practice.

Is there a number with a record of 20 or 28? Find out which record counts are possible, and why they all are multiples of 4.
